content: # From innovation to participation: connectivity and the conduct of contemporary warfareMATTHEW FORD*The smartphone has become the central device for shaping how war is known, represented and conducted. This might sound like hyperbole, but events in Ukraine have revealed how this mundane device is reworking the way society participates in war. It is not just that ordinary civilians can use an app to geolocate an advancing enemy column or pinpoint drone activity. It is also that this one device accelerates both the delivery of military effects and the spread of violent images. There are good reasons why the Ukrainian and Russian armies seek to strip these devices from soldiers as they head to the front line; why Ukraine's security services prosecute civilians for publishing smartphone footage depicting the effects of Russian missile attacks; and why Ukraine's government spends so much time developing influence campaigns designed to shape how people see the war as they head to work in more peaceful parts of the world.<sup>1</sup> Smartphones provide the means both for collecting information in real time and for rapidly disseminating it in ways that directly shape the battlefield. In this respect, smartphones are not simply devices for affecting what the military call the information domain: they also have immediate effects on kinetic activity.This article draws on scholarship in the field of Media Studies to explore the digital mobilization of Ukrainian society. In the process, the article moves discussion away from open innovation to explore the nature of participation in contemporary warfare. What will become apparent is how these changes affect the speed and scale of operations in Ukraine, both at an informational and a kinetic level.Academics have observed how surveillance capitalism works to gather insights on purchasing habits.<sup>2</sup> Algorithms trace an individual's data usage down to the<sup>*</sup> This article is part of a special section in the July 2024 issue of *International Affairs* on 'The crisis in the palm of our hand: smartphones in contexts of conflict and care', guest-edited by Jethro Norman, Signe Marie Cold-Ravnkilde and Matthew Ford. I would like to thank several people for their insights and observations, including Christopher Ankersen, Rupert Barrett-Taylor, Philip W. Blood, Mirjam de Bruijn, Anna Danielsson, Roman Horbyk, Kristin Ljungkvist, Jack McDonald, Per-Erik Nilsson, Aurel Sari, Arthur Snell, Ryan Walsh and Jack Watling. I would also like to thank those working with open-source intelligence, with whom I have been collaborating this past couple of years.<sup>1</sup> See Stephen Fidler and Thomas Grove, 'Smartphones are changing the war in Ukraine: millions of sensors document the conflict, provide targeting information and much else', *Wall Street Journal*, 16 Feb. 2023, https://www.wsj.com/articles/smartphones-are-changing-the-war-in-ukraine-adb37ba1. (Unless otherwise noted at point of citation, all URLs cited in this article were accessible on 24 Jan. 2024.)<sup>2</sup> Shoshana Zuboff, *The age of surveillance capitalism: the fight for a human future at the new frontier of power* (London: Profile Books, 2019).*International Affairs* **100**: 4 (2024) 1531–1549; doi: 10.1093/ia/iiae061© The Author(s) 2024. Published by Oxford University Press on behalf of The Royal Institute of International Affairs. This is an Open Access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), which permits unrestricted reuse, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.---level of geolocating someone on their smartphone doing an online search for a product and directing them to what they might buy in a local shop. Until the war in Ukraine, however, the possibility that these devices could be mobilized for warfighting seems to have been largely left in the marginalia of our thinking. Prior work by the author and Andrew Hoskins establishes something of a framework for considering war in the age of the smartphone.<sup>3</sup> Specifically, their work drew together the idea that the means of war and its representation had collapsed into one register. The smartphone was both a way to represent events and a way to fight—not just in terms of amplifying messages, but also in how citizens engaged in kinetic activity. In this respect, the work took seriously the idea of smartphones as weapons.Ukraine has shown how a mobilized society and a digital ecosystem can be orientated for the purposes of defending a country from invasion. These digital ecosystems form a constitutive part of an evolving 'geometry of power'.<sup>4</sup> Built from a complex web of public and private organizations that needs careful disentanglement, these 'stacks' are shaping a new 'virtual sovereignty'.<sup>5</sup> Much of this sovereignty is dependent on private internet capital and is exercised through digital platforms. Scholars over the last ten years have observed that governments are struggling to keep up with developments in artificial intelligence (AI) compared to the efforts made by the Big Nine tech companies.<sup>6</sup> As Eric Schmidt, the former executive chairman of Alphabet Inc. and the US Department of Defense (DoD)'s Defense Innovation Board, observed in 2018: 'Any military that fails to pursue enterprise-wide cloud computing isn't serious about winning future conflicts. AI is not achievable without modern commercial cloud computing that can store and secure the data DoD regularly collects.'<sup>7</sup> For governments to take advantage of advanced AI, they must therefore work with those private sector companies who are building cloud computing environments and creating the digital platforms, services and smart devices upon which so much of ordinary everyday life now depends.Nevertheless, prior to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and despite a history of civilian smartphone use in conflict that stretches back to at least the 2011 conflict in Libya, the role these devices played in battle rarely featured in thinking about war. It is clear, however, that smartphone technology is playing an increased role in shaping how we come to know and understand war. For example, one NGO documenting war crimes in Ukraine collected 2.8 million digital records between February and May 2022. By contrast, during eleven years of<sup>3</sup> Matthew Ford and Andrew Hoskins, *Radical war: data, attention and control in the 21st century* (London: Hurst, 2022).<sup>4</sup> Benjamin Bratton, *The stack: on software and sovereignty* (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press, 2016), p. 4.<sup>5</sup> Maryanne Kelton et al., 'Virtual sovereignty? Private internet capital, digital platforms and infrastructural power in the United States', *International Affairs* 98: 6, 2022, pp. 1977–99, https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiac226.<sup>6</sup> Amy Webb, *The big nine: how the tech titans and their thinking machines could warp humanity* (New York: PublicAffairs, 2019).<sup>7</sup> Eric Schmidt, 'Statement of Dr Eric Schmidt, House Armed Services Committee, 17 April 2018', United States House of Representatives, https://docs.house.gov/meetings/AS/AS00/20180417/108132/HHRG-115-AS00-Wstate-SchmidtE-20180417.pdf.---war in Syria, the Syrian Archive collected and preserved 5 million digital records.<sup>8</sup> The number of records being produced reflects the extensive availability of the smartphone. At the same time, given this explosion of material, making sense out of it is beyond human comprehension. Instead, sophisticated algorithms must be employed to help analysts search and sift through the records. And yet the availability of AI is unevenly distributed among private sector businesses in different parts of the world. AI is known to harbour latent biases and is rarely available to civil society more broadly.<sup>9</sup> There is, then, an emerging politics of this uneven distribution of technology between those organizations with access to AI and the rest of civil society, which must figure out how to navigate its way through the scale and speed of information being produced about war.However, there is another way of framing contemporary conflict that has its origins in the field of Media Studies. The companies that make AI possible are of course the same companies that provide the information infrastructure which enables people to participate in war. Such infrastructures have, over the past twenty years, disintermediated mainstream media in favour of social media platforms like YouTube and Twitter.<sup>10</sup> Individuals now have the tools to gather, edit and disseminate information in ways that drive political action. These processes have spilled over, not only into how war is reported by mainstream media but also into how soldiers and the public engage in war, and how terrorists organize themselves for maximum propaganda effect.<sup>11</sup> Scholarship in Media Studies has recognized the significance of these changes for how wars are known and understood, calling the process by which people report on and amplify events *participative warfare*. William Merrin defines this to mean a new mode of warfare,where everyone can experience and take part in conflict ... [where] every interested person, of any age, experience, expertise, and qualification, can now fire their own hegemonic bullets in a fractal, digital infowar aimed at exposing their situation or promoting their preferred political interpretation.<sup>12</sup>In this respect participation includes, for example, crowdsourcing activities to buy weapons or map conflict; trolling social media users or publishing personal<sup>8</sup> Fidler and Grove, 'Smartphones are changing the war in Ukraine'.<sup>9</sup> See e.g. John Emery, 'Probabilities towards death: bugsplat, algorithmic assassinations, and ethical due care', *Critical Military Studies* 8: 2, 2022, pp. 179–97, https://doi.org/10.1080/23337486.2020.1809251; James Johnson, 'The AI commander problem: ethical, political, and psychological dilemmas of human–machine interactions in AI-enabled warfare', *Journal of Military Ethics* 21: 3–4, 2022, pp. 246–71, https://doi.org/10.1080/15027570.2 023.2175887.<sup>10</sup> Gerret von Nordheim, Karin Boczek and Lars Koppers, 'Sourcing the sources: an analysis of the use of Twitter and Facebook as a journalistic source over 10 years in the *New York Times*, the *Guardian*, and *Süddeutsche Zeitung*', *Digital Journalism* 6: 7, 2018, pp. 807–28, https://doi.org/10.1080/21670811.2018.1490658.<sup>11</sup> See Kari Andén-Papadopoulos, 'US soldiers imaging the Iraq War on YouTube', *Popular Communication* 7: 1, 2009, pp. 17–27, https://doi.org/10.1080/15405700802584304; Yasmin Ibrahim, 'City under siege: narrating Mumbai through nonstop capture', *Culture Unbound: Journal of Content Cultural Research* 1: 2, 2009, pp. 385–99, http://doi.org/10.3384/cu.2000.1525.09123385; Onook Oh, Manish Agrawal and H. Raghav Rao, 'Information control and terrorism: tracking the Mumbai terrorist attack through Twitter', *Information Systems Frontiers* 13: 1, 2011, pp. 33–43, http://doi.org/10.1007/s10796-010-9275-8; Kevin McSorley, 'Helmetcams, militarized sensation and somatic war', *Journal of War & Culture Studies* 5: 1, 2012, pp. 47–58, https://doi.org/10.1386/jwcs.5.1.47_1; David Kilcullen, *Out of the mountains: the coming age of the urban guerrilla* (London: Hurst, 2013), p. 55.<sup>12</sup> See William Merrin, *Digital war: a critical introduction* (Abingdon and New York: Routledge, 2018), p. 196.---details of adversaries online; or working as a globally distributed diaspora, crowd-sourcing narrative construction to shape the media landscape. This article draws on and contributes to recent debates in Media Studies to bring discussion of innovation and participation into closer alignment, turning the lens from a focus on the armed forces and military-technical change to focus instead on civil society, public engagement and the conduct of war. As this article shows, however, participative warfare has gone beyond the information domain. What has become evident from the start of Russia's 'special military operation' in Ukraine is that civilians are employing digital technology to become directly involved in the actual conduct of war. In effect, participative warfare has gone kinetic. In the process, contemporary technology is helping to collapse distinctions between civilian and soldier, media and weapon.<sup>13</sup>This article seeks to recover some of this narrative, purposely foregrounding smartphone technology in the discussion with a view to stretching thinking about military innovation beyond the current preoccupations with AI and open, or disruptive, innovation.<sup>14</sup> The central claims about the significance of the smartphone are not made to deny the importance of how armed forces and society organize for war. Nor do they suggest, in some technologically determinist sense, that smartphones are somehow more or less important than other military systems. Rather, these claims encourage reflection on how connectivity and conflict are not just the concern of the military, but influence how entire societies will continue to engage with war over the next decade. In this respect, then, the article explores the interlinkages between war and its representation to show how war has become participative in ways that have serious implications for civil society, the laws of armed conflict and the future conduct of warfare.The article proceeds in the following manner. After a discussion of open innovation in the context of defence and military change in Ukraine, the article reflects on parallel scholarly debates on participation in the Media Studies field. These literatures are related to evidence dating back to before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In the process, the goal is to recover a story of digital participation in conflict that stretches back to the era of the global 'war on terror' which began following the 11 September 2001 attacks on the United States. What emerges from this analysis is that Ukraine's digital mobilization represents an evolution of socio-technical changes that has not previously featured in military innovation scholarship. Instead, a preoccupation with AI and roboticization has skewed discussion in ways that underplay the agency of civil society and how it engages with warfare.In the conclusion, the implications of these changes are drawn together. Some features of contemporary conflict—open-source investigations into war crimes, and conflict-mapping—are already understood, even if the standing of these practices has not been formalized in international law.<sup>15</sup> Less well understood are<sup>13</sup> Merrin, *Digital war*, p. 190.<sup>14</sup> For example, see Audrey Kurth Cronin, 'Open source technology and public–private innovation are the key to Ukraine's strategic resilience', *War on the Rocks*, 25 Aug. 2023, https://warontherocks.com/2023/08/open-source-technology-and-public-private-innovation-are-the-key-to-ukraines-strategic-resilience.<sup>15</sup> Sam Dubberley, Alexa Koenig and Darragh Murray, eds, *Digital witness: using open source information for human*1534---*From innovation to participation*the implications that emerge from involving ordinary citizens in reconnaissance and targeting. Who is involved in collecting open-source intelligence (OSINT)? Who are the combatants? Is it legal to engage smartphone-using civilians? How does access to the internet shape what is reported and what becomes admissible for a war crimes tribunal? In these circumstances, this article shifts discussion from innovation towards the way ordinary citizens participate in the conduct of war in the twenty-first century.## From disruptive to open innovationAcademics have traditionally framed military innovation as being driven either from the top down, by army generals and politicians, or from the bottom up, by units adapting while in the heat of battle.<sup>16</sup> Following the US Secretary of State for Defense's announcement of the US Third Offset Strategy in 2014, however, innovation scholars have increasingly sought to contrast the top-down/bottom-up approaches with reference to disruptive innovation or open vs closed innovation. This section briefly explores two decades of military innovation literature, from discussions of military transformation as top-down innovation towards a focus on bottom-up experimentation on the battlefield. These literatures are concerned with the armed forces, non-state actors and those public and private sector organizations that shape military-technical change. As will become apparent, they do not consider the wider question of civil society's participation in war.In terms of definitions, Audrey Kurth Cronin best sums up the difference between open, closed and disruptive innovation. In closed innovation processes, 'state organizations create and control high-end military technologies'. This contrasts with disruptive innovations, which 'shake up existing markets, undercutting the competitive advantage of established industry leaders'. In respect to datafication and the Internet of Things (IoT), the private sector has driven technology change in a way that government could not. If the military is to take advantage of the opportunities these technologies present, then they have to engage more closely with private sector software developers who are otherwise focused on generating profit by selling products to civilian markets.<sup>17</sup> As Christian Brose observes, involving the private sector in developing software for data collection, target acquisition and battle damage assessment is essential.<sup>18</sup> However, increased connectivity has also created the conditions where anyone can develop software or repurpose civilian technology for lethal effect. Now anyone can download the design for a 3D printed gun and make their own plastic firearm. Thus, 'disruptive technologies often democratize access to lethal capabilities, shifting unprec-<sup>16</sup> *rights investigation, documentation, and accountability* (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2020). See Adam Grissom, 'The future of military innovation studies', *Journal of Strategic Studies* 29: 5, 2006, pp. 905–34, https://doi.org/10.1080/01402390600901067.<sup>17</sup> Audrey Kurth Cronin, *Power to the people: how open technological innovation is arming tomorrow's terrorists* (New York: Oxford University Press, 2020), pp. 6, 9, 26.<sup>18</sup> Christian Brose, *The kill chain: defending America in the future of high-tech warfare* (New York: Hachette Group, 2020).1535*International Affairs* 100: 4, 2024---edented power into the hands of civilians.'<sup>19</sup> For Cronin, the US military must embrace open innovation, an approach that 'is driven by commercial processes, not by the military' to avoid getting left behind.<sup>20</sup>The speed of change in relation to disruptive technology contrasts with the rate of innovation during the global 'war on terror'. Innovation studies during the first decade of the twenty-first century showed that top-down defence contracting arrangements designed to deliver 'transformation' could not keep up with events in the field.<sup>21</sup> These programmes were overly bureaucratized, and needed reform if armed forces were to quickly deploy technologies that delivered battle-winning effects. For example, as insurgents in Afghanistan found more low-tech but ingenious ways to bog down American and coalition forces with improvised explosive devices (IEDs), commanders sought ways to increase force protection while interdicting IED supply chains. This reshaped political–military calculations.<sup>22</sup> Out of this battlefield dynamic, academic researchers pointed to the challenges associated with adaptation under fire.<sup>23</sup> This was not about technology driving change so much as the acknowledgement that armed forces had to adjust doctrine and practice in the face of an effective insurgency.<sup>24</sup>Broadly speaking, the scholarship that emerged from the first decade of the 'war on terror' has recognized the significance of bottom-up adaptation for incubating military change.<sup>25</sup> In the decade following the US withdrawal from Iraq, innovation scholarship has subsequently refocused on optimizing adaptation so that war-winning technologies can be deployed more quickly. This has shifted attention to the idea of the battlefield as a place of experimentation. The task is to deploy a working system, understand how it performs in battle and then adapt it, having learned under fire.<sup>26</sup> The principal agents of this approach to innovation have been the US special operations forces, who have been most preoccupied with managing the global 'war on terror' following withdrawal from Iraq and drawdown in Afghanistan. To help them deploy new technologies, they established an external incubator called SOFWERX—designed, according to Nina Kollars, 'to improve the agility and performance of its technology acquisitions<sup>19</sup> Cronin, *Power to the people*, p. 7.<sup>20</sup> Audrey Kurth Cronin, 'Technology and strategic surprise: adapting to an era of open innovation', *Parameters* 50: 3, 2020, pp. 71–84 at p. 72, http://doi.org/10.55540/0031-1723.2675.<sup>21</sup> See Peter Dombrowski and Eugene Gholz, *Buying military transformation: technology innovation and the defense industry* (New York: Columbia University Press, 2003); James Russell, *Innovation, transformation and war: counterinsurgency operations in Anbar and Ninewa provinces, Iraq, 2005–2007* (Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 2011); Nina Kollars, 'Military innovation's dialectic: gun trucks and rapid acquisition', *Security Studies* 23: 4, 2014, pp. 787–813, https://doi.org/10.1080/09636412.2014.965000.<sup>22</sup> Mark Clegg, 'Force protection and society', *Defense & Security Analysis* 28: 2, 2012, pp. 131–9, https://doi.org/ 10.1080/14751798.2012.678150.<sup>23</sup> See Robert Foley, Stuart Griffin and Helen McCartney, 'Transformation in contact: learning the lessons of modern war', *International Affairs* 87: 2, 2011, pp. 253–70, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2346.2011.00972.x.<sup>24</sup> John A. Nagl, *Learning to eat soup with a knife: counterinsurgency lessons from Malaya and Vietnam* (Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Press, 2005).<sup>25</sup> Michael Horowitz and Shira C. Pindyck, 'What is a military innovation and why it matters', *Journal of Strategic Studies* 46: 1, 2023, pp. 85–114, https://doi.org/10.1080/01402390.2022.2038572.<sup>26</sup> Jon R. Lindsay, 'Reinventing the revolution: technological visions, counterinsurgent criticism, and the rise of special operations', *Journal of Strategic Studies* 36: 3, 2013, pp. 422–53, https://doi.org/10.1080/01402390.2012 .734252.---process'.27 As part of a constellation of innovation incubators associated with the DoD's Defense Innovation Unit, the goal was to leverage 'commercial off-the-shelf technology to extend the battlefield and win the fight for information'.28In contrast with the innovation literature from the early 2000s, more recent studies have critically engaged with how software exploits existing sources of data collection or integrates processes and new sensors with older established military platforms.29 These literatures have studied the way innovations optimize target selection, situational awareness and logistics provision.30 The literature that emerged from this process stemmed from the other main innovation that came out of the 'war on terror', the evolution of targeting activities associated with the Joint Special Operations Command under General Stanley McChrystal.31 While earlier conceptualizations of military adaptation focused on mass and protection, studies of the approach taken by McChrystal led to a shift in framing innovation towards accelerating the speed at which military effects could be produced.32 Although the precise implications for how the armed forces ought to transform themselves is contested,33 this has spawned a separate literature drawing on ideas associated with optimizing information collection and distribution, flat organization structures and 'hackathon' problem-solving events as a way to drive open innovation.34 Armed forces must embrace these ways of working. If they do not, then they risk a shift in power 'from dominant players to surprise actors in ways that change the overall shape of the marketplace of violence'.35The present war in Ukraine creates an opportunity to investigate the relative merits of these different models of innovation and socio-technical change. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukraine had been unable to buy offensive weapons and engage with western arms manufacturers. As a result, Ukraine had to develop its own military innovation ecosystem.36 Schmidt argues that Ukraine's battle-27 Nina Kollars, 'SOFWERX's return on collision: measuring open collaborative innovation', *Special Operations Journal* 3: 1, 2017, pp. 11–20, https://doi.org/10.1080/23296151.2017.1310593.28 Adam Jay Harrison, Bharat Rao and Bala Mulloth, 'Developing an innovation-based ecosystem at the U.S. Department of Defense: challenges and opportunities', *Defense Horizons* 81: 1, 2017, https://inss.ndu.edu/Portals/68/Documents/defensehorizon/DH-81.pdf, pp. 1–15; Benjamin Jensen, 'Think bigger: the third offset and extending the battlefield', *War on the Rocks*, 12 Dec. 2016, https://warontherocks.com/2016/12/think-bigger-the-third-offset-and-extending-the-battlefield.29 Jon R. Lindsay, *Information technology and military power* (Ithaca, NY: Cornell University Press, 2020).30 See Matthew Ford and Alex Gould, 'From warrior geek to prototype warrior: entrepreneurialism, future war, and the emergence of twenty-first century civil-military relations', *Digital War*, no. 2, 2021, pp. 35–50, https://doi.org/10.1057/s42984-021-00039-w.31 Stanley McChrystal, 'It takes a network—the new front line of modern warfare', *Foreign Policy*, 21 Feb. 2011, https://foreignpolicy.com/2011/02/21/it-takes-a-network.32 Jon R. Lindsay, 'War upon the map: user innovation in American military software', *Technology and Culture* 51: 3, 2010, pp. 619–51, http://doi.org/10.1353/tech.2010.0027.33 Patrick Bury, 'US Special Forces transformation: post-Fordism and the limits of networked warfare', *International Affairs* 98: 2, 2022, pp. 587–607, https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiab213.34 Phil Zimmerman, Tracee Gilbert and Frank Salvatore, 'Digital engineering transformation across the Department of Defense', *The Journal of Defense Modelling and Simulation* 16: 4, 2019, pp. 325–38, https://doi.org/10.1177/1548512917747050; Audrey Kurth Cronin, 'Technology and strategic surprise: adapting to an era of open innovation', *Parameters* 50: 3, 2020, pp. 71–84, http://doi.org/10.55540/0031-1723.2675.35 Cronin, *Power to the people*, p. 178.36 Deborah Sanders, 'Ukraine's third wave of military reform 2016–2022—building a military able to defend Ukraine against the Russian invasion', *Defence & Security Analysis* 39: 3, 2023, pp. 312–28, https://doi.org/10.1080/14751798.2023.2201017.---## Participative warfareDescribed by Andrew Hoskins and Pavel Shchelin as 'the war feed', representations of war are now being shaped continuously, at scale and in highly personalized ways across a multitude of social media platforms involving billions of participants all over the world.38 The speed and level at which interaction takes place is beyond human comprehension. At the same time, even with the help of advanced AI, social media platforms struggle to retain control over what content is posted and taken down. AI tools misidentify posts that conform with platform policy and then take this material down while leaving content that violates platform guidelines online available for everyone to see. In this context, different users have unique opportunities to post, like and amplify their war feeds in ways that may or may not lead to shared understanding with people in their wider networks. NGOs, intelligence agencies and those private sector firms who are processing this vast quantity of data claim a more systematic window on events depicted through the prisms of online life. Meanwhile, ordinary participants in the war feed struggle to make sense of the overload of images and material that they now witness. This disparity of understanding and its effects on politics is poorly understood.The history of how war and its representation came to this point reflects the changing media ecosystems of the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.39 The way mainstream print and broadcast media work is intimately connected to constitutional rights and protections associated with freedom of speech and of the press, and with libel law. Corroborating sources and fact-checking inevitably demands editorial process and oversight, which takes time and resources. Historical processes have produced different attitudes towards journalism and media in different parts of the world. Social media, by contrast, is less than twenty years old, and has been layered into these different media ecosystems at different points37 Eric Schmidt, 'Innovation power: why technology will define the future of geopolitics', *Foreign Affairs*, 102: 2, 2023, https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/eric-schmidt-innovation-power-technology-geopolitics.38 Andrew Hoskins and Pavel Shchelin, 'The war feed: digital war in plain sight', *American Behavioral Scientist* 67: 3, 2023, pp. 449–63, https://doi.org/10.1177/00027642221144848.39 Olga Boichak and Andrew Hoskins, 'My war: participation in warfare', *Digital War*, no. 3, 2022, pp. 1–8, https://doi.org/10.1057/s42984-022-00060-7.---in time with differing degrees of state oversight. This has complicated existing information spaces, creating even more diverse media cultures and legal frameworks. Each of the thirty-odd local, regional and global social media platforms has its own subculture, demographic profile and approach to online engagement. Smartphone functionality means that users can post content more quickly than broadcast media, instantly gathering feedback on how well it is received. No editorial process is required, and so the speed at which people can engage and stories can 'go viral' has accelerated. As several authors, including Peter Singer, Emerson Brooking and David Patrikarakos have observed, this phenomenon is having an impact not just on how war is represented but also on how it is fought.<sup>40</sup>While it is clear that connectivity shapes participation in violence, the complexity of these media ecosystems presents challenges for academic researchers and makes systematic study extremely difficult.<sup>41</sup> Recognizing this complexity, Media Studies has sought to make sense out of the changing information ecology—or what we reframe for this special section as the *global crisis ecology*<sup>42</sup>—and how it frames what we know and understand about war. Thus, the field turns the direction of enquiry away from explaining processes of military change and instead looks at how we can make knowledge claims in complex media environments. This takes us from ontological assertions about the rights and wrongs of innovation and good military science towards an epistemological question about the limits of knowledge under digital conditions. In this respect, the field draws attention to how everyday engagement in online life shapes what we understand and believe about war. By examining the systems that make these connections possible, the importance of ordinary people's online participation in war, both at an ephemeral and a meaningful level, is foregrounded. As people interact online, they amplify perceptions in ways that may or may not accord with shared truths, but which nonetheless still produce change in attitudes and behaviours.In this respect, Media Studies starts with an acknowledgement that we now live in a deeply mediatized world where everyday experience is digitally saturated.<sup>43</sup> This is the product of a process of datafication in which ordinary aspects of life are being turned into online quantifiable data points.<sup>44</sup> Forming the digital backbone of the IoT, 5G mobile networks are rapidly accelerating this process. All of this depends on an unevenly distributed information infrastructure that represents a<sup>40</sup> David Patrikarakos, *War in 140 characters: how social media is reshaping conflict in the twenty-first century* (New York: Basic Books, 2017); P. W. Singer and Emerson T. Brooking, *LikeWar: the weaponization of social media* (Boston: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2018).<sup>41</sup> Peter Chonka, Abdirahman Edle Ali and Kirsti Sturvøy, 'Eyes on the ground and eyes in the sky: security narratives, participatory visual methods and knowledge production in danger zones', *Security Dialogue* 53: 6, 2022, pp. 567–88, https://doi.org/10.1177/09670106221111620.<sup>42</sup> See Jethro Norman, Matthew Ford and Signe Marie Cold-Ravnkilde, 'The crisis in the palm of our hand', *International Affairs* 100: 4, 2024, pp. 1361–79, https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiae128; Jethro Norman, 'Platform kinship and the reshaping of political order in the Somali territories', *International Affairs* 100: 4, 2024, pp. 1431–1450, https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiae134; Signe Marie Cold-Ravnkilde and Almamy Sylla, 'The rise of Mali's new videomen as cybercombatants in the global crisis ecology', *International Affairs* 100: 4, 2024, pp. 1405–29, https://doi.org/10.1093/ia/iiae121.<sup>43</sup> Andreas Hepp, *Deep mediatization* (Abingdon and New York: Routledge, 2020).<sup>44</sup> Viktor Mayer-Schönberger and Kenneth Cukier, *Big data: a revolution that will transform how we live, work and think* (Boston: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2013).---compound of people, processes, organizations, and technical systems that includes the services and technologies that make up the internet.<sup>45</sup> These infrastructures obviously provide the basis for connections between humans. At the same time, however, these interconnections are themselves shaped by the information infrastructures that make these interactions possible. This 'figuration' of reality demands close attention, because it frames the limits of people's participation in the multiple and interlocking information grids that emerge from differing access to the web and to social and mainstream media.<sup>46</sup> This process of figuration acts to mould the way in which different interpersonal online interactions are amplified. Highly connected populations with a low-latency telecoms grid produce a different structure of knowledge from populations of countries or regions where it is possible to connect to the internet but where the availability of a smartphone is limited to one in three people on a 3G network.In war, this is important because it shapes what can be known and how viable civilian information infrastructures can be for warfighting purposes. This is not just about warfighting in what western armed forces would describe as an information domain: it also has very practical effects in how society organizes for and participates in war.<sup>47</sup> The NGO Bellingcat is a good example of how volunteer teams investigate events to identify how armed forces have been engaged in war crimes. In the first instance, it is important to note that the war in Ukraine has gone through several phases. Early in the invasion, civilian involvement in intelligence-gathering played a more prominent role than it did during periods when the front lines stabilized. It is also apparent that the precise gearing of interactions between civilian smartphone technology, social media and the intelligence collection/fusion cycle employed by Ukraine's armed forces needs further research. However, it is evident that Ukrainian citizens are directly participating in the process of finding, locating and targeting Russian armed forces. In effect, Ukraine has provided the tools to help its citizens resist invasion and occupation. The problem is that by participating in this way, civilians become combatants and become legal targets for Russian attacks.<sup>82</sup> Indeed, Ukrainians with targeting apps loaded onto their smartphones have been rounded up and killed for behaving like combatants. This is principally because these citizens have become a part of the Ukrainian kill chain. According to Chris Brose, this advances in three stages, starting with processing intelligence to understand enemy activities, followed by deciding on how to respond. It finishes by taking action to achieve a political effect. By providing information-gathering tools to ordinary citizens,<sup>83</sup> the Ukrainian kill chain has become more resilient, but the forfeit for this has been the loss of civilian status in war.Open-source investigation NGOs like Bellingcat and Mnemonic have been instrumental in establishing the use of digital sources for war crimes purposes. Although datafication ought in theory to make prosecuting war crimes easier, the enormous quantities of data being produced presents evidentiary challenges for international war crimes tribunals.<sup>84</sup> These challenges include the task of forensically verifying the veracity of images and video, and making sure that all the organizations and people involved in documenting criminality are working to the same standards of verification. While Clearview is taking sides in the conflict, its technology is unlikely to be viewed as a legitimate source of evidence by Russia. Using sophisticated forms of AI to try to make sense of the data overload is unlikely to help sustain faith in international processes of justice. Rather, we are currently watching the splintering of information infrastructures, as China and the United States advance their geopolitical interests in favour of separating the internet into different so called 'splinternets'. Even more problematically, the accidental archives created out of the recordings from the battlefield also imply the possibility of infinitely targeting individuals at some future point.For those thinking through what it means to fight in hybrid or sub-threshold warfare, smartphone-enabled participative warfare presents new opportunities for attacking and resisting adversaries. On the one hand, it creates new avenues for data collection.<sup>88</sup> At the same time, it creates more resilient targeting processes. Controlling this type of activity will not be easy in this scenario. One might argue that platform providers like Google or Apple could prevent people from participating in conflict by denying access to apps intended for warfighting. However, as the internet splinters along geopolitical lines, the use of virtual private networks (VPNs) and a proliferation of providers make it unlikely that participative warfare can merely be 'switched off' at any future point.## ConclusionThis article has refocused discussion on the conduct of contemporary warfare away from the challenges posed by innovation and towards those that emerge out of participation. Participative warfare blurs the lines between civilian and soldier, between what is public and what is private. The smartphone is an important technology that shapes these practices. As part of the targeting cycle, the smartphone becomes a node in a distributed kill chain. In the process, its use further collapses the distinction between media and weapon.This implies that civilian and military information infrastructures are now so deeply intertwined that the politics of violence has already undergone a reshaping. In this respect, participative warfare creates modes of representation in which private companies and intelligence agencies claim to be able to read the battlefield in real time, while public experience is distorted by the social media prisms that purport to explain how war is unfolding. This asymmetry of understanding has created the conditions for the social media crowdsourcing of intelligence. Crowdsourced OSINT does not have to depend on the kinds of AI tools available to big tech, and yet its influence on the understanding of war has been profound. Far from reducing the fog of war, however, OSINT cannot overcome sensory overload or, paradoxically, the associated sense of ennui that comes from having access to vast quantities of information.Given the general public's concerns about AI-enabled weapons, it would be easy to focus on the innovation ecosystem as the most salient feature of the technological changes currently under way in Ukraine. However, if we focus too much attention on what it means to innovate without reflecting on the way that civilians are newly enrolled in the digital battlefield, then we miss the obvious<sup>88</sup> Paul Burke, 'The issues in the collection, verification and actionability of citizen-derived crowdsourced intelligence during the invasion of Ukraine, 2022', *Strategic Panorama*, 2022, pp. 94–103, https://doi.org/10.53679/2616-9460.specialissue.2022.09.---*From innovation to participation*point that connected devices make possible new forms of mass participation in war. People produce, broadcast and consume information all from one connected device. They—often unwittingly—create an enormous amount of data that is being used for military purposes. This process is worthy of study on its own terms, and extends simple discussions of military innovation beyond the current preoccupations with cyber warfare and different forms of AI.When these changes are placed in a broader historical context, the war in Ukraine implies a need to break with previous framings of warfare. The Industrial Revolution which transformed economies across Europe and North America also led to the advent of total war. Civilians entered into the war effort, being mobilized for the purposes of mass production. This home front became subject to strategic attack through aerial bombardment and helped frame the LOAC as it is currently understood. By contrast, the IoT makes it possible to digitally mobilize society in the defence of the state. This shift occurs in the realm of informational reality, where anyone can amplify war-related content. At the same time, large-scale connectivity has turned every individual with a smartphone into a component of a larger digital kill chain. The scale of involvement and the speed at which civilians can participate wherever they are in the world implies the need for contemporary warfare to be reframed to to include notions of digital war.We need to be alive to the challenges this creates, precisely because Schmidt, a longstanding influence on big tech, is urging the United States to create an enormous 'constellation of sensors' and 'focus more on open-source intelligence, given that most of the world's data today is publicly available'.<sup>89</sup> In this scenario, the state will seek to leverage open sources of data in ways that will create resilient kill chains. How wider digital transformations in civil society affect the way that armed forces are organized is yet to be defined. It is likely, however, that the data produced by ordinary citizens will ensure everyone participates in the state's efforts to render the battlefield transparent. If these practices are to remain under democratic oversight, the nature of participation—and the complexity of contemporary information infrastructures that underpin it—need more detailed research. Events in Ukraine imply that participative warfare is now an everyday feature of twenty-first-century conflict.<sup>89</sup> Schmidt, 'Innovation power'.

metadata.title: From innovation to participation: connectivity and the conduct of contemporary warfare
metadata.abstract: The war in Ukraine is the first conventional war to ever take place in an entirely connected information ecology. The internet has not been switched off. Mundane smart devices are ubiquitous. Soldiers and ordinary civilians are participating in the conflict in ways that have never previously been possible. This stretches participation beyond the information domain and the kinds of connectivity that shaped conflicts in places like Syria, Tigray and Mali. Now the smartphone is routinely being used by soldiers and civilians alike to geolocate enemy columns, control drones to range find for artillery, and produce and broadcast the damage assessment for online audiences to watch. Surveillance technology already makes it possible to track individual smartphone users. In times of peace these forms of surveillance are curtailed. During a conventional war, however, private organizations and governments have reason to circumvent peacetime legal conventions.
